rows.title: Plain words: exposed is not contaminated
rows.hook: Two words people mix up. They mean different things. One ends when you step away.

blocks.text: Two words get swapped all the time. Exposed. Contaminated. They are not the same thing.
Exposed
You are exposed when you are in the path of radiation from a source. A medical X-ray is a source outside the body. When the radiation stops reaching you, the exposure is over.
Contaminated
Contamination is radioactive material on or in something, where it is not wanted. On skin or clothes. Breathed in. Swallowed. Spread about a place.
Radiation does not get on or in people. The material is what spreads.

blocks.caption: Left: a hand in the path of radiation. Right: material on a hand, being rinsed off.

blocks.text: Material on skin or clothes can often be washed off. Exposure to a source outside you ends when the source is shielded or you move away.

items: Exposed: in the path of radiation from a source
Contaminated: radioactive material is on or in you

blocks.text: A sealed source keeps its material inside its container. Material that is not sealed might be spread onto other things. That is the part to watch.
Say it right. Exposed to radiation. Contaminated with material. Different problem, different fix.

rows.title: nobody knows when
rows.hook: one unstable nucleus is a surprise. a whole crowd of them follows a pattern. isn't that neat?

blocks.text: ok so take one unstable nucleus. leave it alone. it has a chance of changing, and nobody can say when. eep, so mysterious~
nobody pushes it. the nucleus that changes is the parent. the nucleus it becomes is the daughter. the change gives off radiation
a half-life ticks for a crowd of atoms, never for one
think of a die
roll a die once and you can't say if it will show a six. roll it 600 times and you can say that about 100 of the rolls will. hehe
a nucleus is like that. one is a surprise. a big group follows a pattern, and in the half-life lesson you'll see the pattern for yourself. it's so pretty~

blocks.caption: The radiation sign, used to mark a source of radiation.

blocks.text: Scientists noticed that the radiation does not change with the chemical state of the material, or with temperature or pressure. That is a clue that it comes from the nucleus, not from the electrons.

items: One nucleus: you can't say when
A big group: it follows a pattern

blocks.text: so when someone asks you when an atom will change, you can say: you can't know. a crowd of them, though, you can know. hehe, tiny mystery solved~

blocks.label: see what comes out of a decay

rows.title: Calm note: reading a scary number
rows.hook: A frightening headline is only a number. Three questions make it something you can judge.

blocks.text: You read a headline about radiation, and your stomach drops. That is a normal reaction. Here is what I do next. I slow down and ask three questions.
Three questions

items: How big is the dose, in millisieverts?
How fast did it arrive?
How does it compare with doses I already know?

blocks.caption: A page with a headline, and a lens held over its number.

blocks.text: Two answers that are both wrong
One says any dose of radiation is deadly. The other says radiation is harmless. Neither is right.
Size and speed decide what a dose does.

A very large dose in a short time can make people ill, with symptoms such as nausea and vomiting within hours. Low levels do not cause immediate health effects, but they can add a small increase in the risk of cancer over a lifetime.
Cells are extremely efficient at repairing radiation damage. If a dose is low, or spread over a long time, the risk is lower because repair is more likely.
So next time, take a breath and ask the three questions. A number with a size, a speed and something to compare it with is much easier to hold.

rows.title: the banana on your counter
rows.hook: a banana is a little bit radioactive. so are you. that's normal, and here's why

blocks.text: ok here's something nobody expects. the banana on your counter is a little bit radioactive. surprise~
it holds potassium, and a tiny share of that potassium is potassium-40, which is unstable. you carry some too, in your own body
it was here first
radioactivity wasn't invented. it was here long before people were. you can find it in four places

items: Rocks and soil: uranium and thorium
The air: radon, a radioactive gas from the ground
Food and your body: potassium-40
Space: cosmic radiation, all the time

blocks.caption: A banana holds a little natural potassium-40.

blocks.text: radioactivity was always here. we only learned to see it

In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that a uranium-rich rock gives off invisible rays that darken a photographic plate, even inside an enclosed container. Radioactivity was found in a natural material, long before anyone built nuclear technology.
is it dangerous?
radioactive doesn't automatically mean dangerous. what matters is the type of radiation, how much there is, and how it reaches the body.
a banana and your own body are radioactive, and that's normal. later you'll learn why being exposed to radiation isn't the same as becoming radioactive.

blocks.label: find where radioactivity hides around you

rows.title: Plain words: a detector always finds a little
rows.hook: Switch one on in an empty field and it still reads something. That is background.

blocks.text: You switch on a detector. Nothing nearby. It still reads a little. Nothing is wrong with it.
Background

Background radiation is present on Earth at all times. It comes mostly from natural minerals in the ground, soil and water, and from cosmic radiation. A working detector picks up a little almost anywhere.

blocks.caption: A counter reads a little among rock, grass, water and sunlight.

blocks.text: A reading above zero does not mean something is wrong.
Background radiation varies from place to place on Earth, so what a detector picks up varies too.
What a Geiger counter does

Radiation ionizes the gas inside the tube. The rate of ionization goes with the amount of radiation. More radiation, more ionization to detect. A scintillation counter turns flashes of light into a signal. A dosimeter is worn to measure how much radiation a person is exposed to.

items: Geiger counter: detects radiation
Scintillation counter: turns flashes of light into a signal
Dosimeter: worn, measures how much a person is exposed to

blocks.text: So read the number against the background. Know the normal first. Then you can tell when something is different.

blocks.label: go over the three units again

rows.title: Calm note: the dose you already get
rows.hook: You get a little radiation every day, and so does everyone else. Here is how much.

blocks.text: If radiation worries you a little, that is fine. A lot of people feel that way. Let's start with something steady: you are already getting a small dose, every day, and so is everyone you know.
How it is counted
A dose is counted in sieverts. Everyday doses are tiny, so they are usually given in millisieverts. One sievert is 1000 millisieverts.
An ordinary year
In the United States the average person gets about 6.2 millisieverts a year. Most of it is natural background radiation.

blocks.caption: A dial with its needle resting in the low zone, and the everyday sources round it: sun, rock, grass and water.

blocks.text: Most of our average yearly dose comes from natural background radiation.
A whole body CT scan is about 10 millisieverts. About 1000 millisieverts in a short time is where people start to become ill.

items: Living near a nuclear power station for a year: under 0.01 millisieverts
Cosmic radiation at sea level for a year: about 0.3 millisieverts
Radon in an average home for a year: about 2.3 millisieverts

blocks.text: A number only means something when you put it next to the ones you know. That is all a scale is for.

rows.title: The smallest thing you will ever meet
rows.hook: You have never seen one, yet you are made of them. Let us look at how small they really are.

blocks.text: Look at your hand. Now look at the air around it. Both are matter, and all matter is made of atoms.

Yes, even the air, which gives every impression of being nothing. That is why you can pump up a ball: the air inside it takes up space, because air is matter too. I have weighed several balls to be certain. The neighbours have asked me to stop.
Small things are best looked at slowly. I still look at them every day.
How small is small?
An atom is about 10^-10 m across, one ten-billionth of a metre. The nucleus in its middle is about 100,000 times smaller still.

blocks.caption: An atom: far too small to see.

items: An atom: about 10^-10 m across
Its nucleus: about 100,000 times smaller

blocks.text: In the fifth century BC the Greek thinkers Leucippus and Democritus argued that all matter was made of small pieces they called atomos, a word for "indivisible". Seeing atoms took far longer.
So the next time you pick something up, remember that you are holding a huge crowd of atoms you can never see. Take a moment with that. I will wait.

blocks.label: Zoom in on an atom yourself

rows.title: Three kinds of carbon
rows.hook: Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 are all carbon. One of them is not like the others. Let us see which.

blocks.text: Here is a puzzle. Three atoms are all carbon, yet they are not the same. How can that be? Let us count.
Count the protons. Every carbon atom has 6, and that number is what makes it carbon. Change it and you get a different element.
The neutrons are the difference
The number after the name is the mass number: protons plus neutrons. Carbon has 6 protons, so carbon-14 has 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons. I checked the subtraction. Twice.

items: Carbon-12: 6 protons, 6 neutrons, stable
Carbon-13: 6 protons, 7 neutrons, stable
Carbon-14: 6 protons, 8 neutrons, unstable

blocks.text: These versions of one element are called isotopes. Most of the atoms around you are stable isotopes.
Isotope does not mean radioactive. It only means a different number of neutrons.
Carbon-14 is the unstable one. An unstable nucleus can change, and when it does it gives off radiation. That is called radioactivity.
Even so, nothing here is strange or new. Unstable atoms are in rocks, in the air and in food, and they were here long before us. The rocks have been very patient about it.
Which brings a question. What exactly comes out when a nucleus changes? Ada knows. She tells it brightly. Please be prepared.
